title: How to respond to real estate leads faster on Mac: a realtor's routine that works
metaTitle: Respond to Real Estate Leads Faster on Mac for Realtors
description: Buyers often reach out to several agents. Learn what slow replies cost, why they happen, and free Mac fixes to respond to real estate leads faster.
targetKeyword: respond to real estate leads faster
secondaryKeywords: answer new real estate leads faster
realtor lead follow up on Mac

intro: To respond to real estate leads faster, cut the gap between a lead arriving and your first reply. For most realtors, that gap comes from notification settings, Focus modes, and batch inbox checks. This page covers what slow replies cost, why they happen, and fixes you can use on your Mac today, before you buy anything.
tldr: Buyers often reach out to more than one agent. A fast, useful reply keeps you in the conversation.
Most slow replies come from notification settings, Focus filters, and checking mail in batches.
Point all lead mail at one mailbox, turn on its alerts, allow Mail in your showing Focus, and save Gmail templates.
Log arrival and reply times in Google Sheets for a few weeks before you change tools.
Lazur drafts and dictates replies and points at buttons. You still read, edit, and send every message yourself.

blocks.text: Here is a common week, as an example and not a study. A portal sends a buyer inquiry at ten in the morning. You are in a listing appointment until lunch. You open your inbox at three in the afternoon and find the buyer has already booked a showing with another agent. Nobody did anything wrong on purpose. The reply simply came late.
What slow replies cost you

The cost is more than one lost lead. Buyers often reach out to several agents at once. The agent who answers the first question usually gets the next question, the showing time, and the early trust. HBR's 2011 article 'The Short Life of Online Sales Leads' says it plainly: 'Our research shows that most companies are not responding nearly fast enough.' The page gave no sample size or response times, so read it as a direction, not a measured rate.

You will see bigger claims online, with multiples and percentages attached to fast replies. I could not trace those numbers to a primary study, so this page leaves them out. Your own log is a better source. It shows your gap, your lead sources, and your slow days. Start that log before you buy anything.

Your hours are a cost too. NAR's 2026 member profile reports a median of 35 hours per week for all Realtors, and 30 hours for sales agents. Brokers and managers who sell report 40 to 45 hours. Those hours already hold showings, calls, and paperwork. A lead that waits in your inbox does not stop taking time. It often comes back later, when you have even less room for it.
Why new leads wait so long

Most delays come from setup, not from willpower. The Bureau of Labor Statistics says 55% of brokers and 54% of sales agents are self-employed. Their schedules often include evenings and weekends, and many hours are irregular. If you work alone, no teammate reads the inbox while you are on a showing. The delay is built into the day.

The first setup problem is notifications. In Mail, open Mail > Settings > General and look at the New message notifications pop-up. That is where you choose which mailbox triggers alerts. If your lead mailbox is not the one chosen there, new messages may arrive without a banner or a sound. You can keep the app open and still miss the lead for most of a morning.

The second problem is Focus. A Focus can hide alerts you did not expect. Apple's Focus guide lets you set notifications to Allow Some People or Allow Some Apps. A Focus can also include a Mail filter that decides which email accounts appear during it. If you set up a showing Focus months ago and never revisited it, your lead account may be hidden. Check it on the day you need it, not after the lead is gone.

The third problem is habit. Many agents check mail in batches. That works for newsletters, but it is slow for leads. Leads also arrive in several places. A portal, a website form, a text, and a voicemail transcript can each hold a buyer. The place you check least will be the slowest one.
Fixes you can use today without buying anything

Start with one lead mailbox. Route portal and website form mail there if your setup allows it. Then set the notifications, set the Focus, and save templates. These fixes cost nothing beyond your time. You can test each one in the same afternoon, and you will know quickly if it worked.

items: Choose one lead mailbox and turn on its alerts in Mail > Settings > General.
Open the Focus you use for showings. Set notifications to Allow Some Apps, then add Mail.
Write three Gmail templates: a first reply, a showing time request, and a check-in note.
Create a Shortcut with an Email trigger that sends you a notification. Test it with a message from another account.
Log each lead in Google Sheets with its arrival time and first reply time.
On busy days, send a short holding reply before you can give a full answer.

blocks.text: Shortcuts on Mac can run automatically when an email arrives. Apple's guide lists Email among the automation triggers, next to Time of Day and Do Not Disturb. Keep the first version simple. A notification is enough to start. Apple's guide also says that if you turn on Allow Running When Locked, the automation will not notify you when it runs. Keep that option off for any automation you need to see.

Gmail templates fix repeat typing faster than anything else on this list. Write the reply you send most often, once, and save it. Your first reply should ask one question and offer a time. Keep it short. A short reply that goes out now beats a perfect one that goes out tomorrow. For setup steps, see [Gmail for realtors on Mac](/for/realtors/gmail).
A reply log in Google Sheets that shows the gap

Make a sheet with columns for lead name, source, arrival time, first reply time, and reply gap. Subtract arrival time from first reply time, then format that cell as a duration. Fill in the log every time a lead comes in. It takes less time than searching your inbox later to reconstruct what happened.

After a few weeks, sort by the gap. You will see which source is slow, which day is slow, and which mailbox is slow. Fix the worst one first. In most cases it is one setting, one filter, or one habit. For sheet help, see [Google Sheets for realtors on Mac](/for/realtors/google-sheets).

blocks.text: Lead response time on a busy showing day

Showing days are where the gap grows. You are driving, walking through houses, and talking with sellers. Plan for that day before it starts. Keep your showing Focus on, but let Mail through. Check the log at the start of the day and again at the end. If a lead arrives in the middle, send a holding reply and say you will follow up with specific times that evening.

A holding reply is not a full answer. It tells the buyer you saw the message, and it keeps the conversation open. Keep it under three sentences. Do not guess at price, availability, or terms. Those details belong in your follow-up, where you can check them against the listing.
Where Lazur helps, and where it does not

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that lives in the notch. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. Ask where a button is, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it. Hold fn to dictate clean text at the cursor in any app. Lazur helps most with the wording of a reply. It can also guide you through settings, one click at a time.

Lazur does not send emails for you. It does not click buttons or operate other apps. It is not a plugin or add-in for Gmail, and it has no partnership with Gmail or any other app maker. You read the draft, edit it, and press Send yourself. Lazur drafts and types text. It does not decide what the buyer should hear.

Try this test on your next real inquiry. Open the message, hold ⌥ ⌘, and ask what the buyer wants. Then ask for a short first reply that asks one question and offers a showing time. Check the price, address, and availability yourself. Lazur only knows what is on your screen at that moment.

Dictation is the other half. Hold fn and speak your reply into any text box, including Gmail. Speaking can be quicker than typing a long answer, so compare the two on a few real replies. Dictation is unlimited on both the Pro and Power plans. Keep your edits light, and read the result before you send it.
Privacy and client data before you use any AI tool

If your brokerage has rules about client data, follow them before you paste a buyer's details into any tool. Ask your broker which tools are allowed. Some details, like a phone number or a loan figure, may need extra care. Keep the lead log to the minimum you need to measure reply time.

Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Lazur keeps a memory of what you asked and did, on your Mac.
Paid tools, and what they cost

A CRM is the next step when leads arrive in too many places to track by hand. Follow Up Boss lists its Grow plan at $69 per user per month on monthly billing, or $58 per user on annual billing. Calling is a $39 per user add-on on monthly billing, or $33 on annual billing. Its Pro plan is $499 per month, including 10 users. Prices exclude tax and may change, so check their pricing page.

No study I found shows that a specific tool speeds up replies for realtors. Vendor pages make that claim, but they are marketing. Use your reply log to test any tool for a few weeks before you commit. Compare the gap before and after. Keep the tool only if the gap shrinks.
Mistakes that keep replies slow

items: Turning off all notifications to stop distraction, then forgetting to check the inbox.
Writing a long first reply when one short question would start the conversation.
Sharing one inbox across portals, past clients, and vendors, so leads get buried.
Building a Shortcut and never testing it with a real email.
Sending a reply with a wrong price or address because you typed too fast.
Ignoring weekend leads because your phone is set to quiet.
Measuring nothing, then buying a tool to fix a setting problem.

blocks.text: Start with the mailbox, then the Focus, then the templates. Those three changes touch the most common delays, and they take less than an afternoon. The log tells you if they worked. Keep the log running after you finish this page, because the gap changes when your lead sources change.

faq.question: How fast should I respond to a new real estate lead?
faq.answer: I could not verify a single target from a primary study, so this page does not give one. Set your own target. Measure your reply gap for a few weeks in a log, then improve the slowest source first.

faq.question: Does Lazur send the reply for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur drafts and dictates text, and it points at buttons. It does not click send, click buttons, or operate other apps. You read the reply, edit it, and send it yourself.

faq.question: Do I need a CRM to respond faster?
faq.answer: No. Mail notifications, a Focus that allows Mail, Gmail templates, and a Google Sheets log cover the basics. A CRM helps when leads arrive in many places. Check the pricing page of any CRM before you commit.

faq.question: What if a lead arrives while I am showing a house?
faq.answer: Send a short holding reply. Say you are with a client and will follow up with specific times. Do not guess at price, availability, or terms in the holding reply.

faq.question: Is it safe to paste lead details into an AI tool?
faq.answer: Follow your brokerage's rules on client data first. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and screenshots go to AI providers to answer and are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models.

faq.question: Why not turn on alerts for every email?
faq.answer: Alerts for every email create noise, and you start ignoring them. Pick one lead mailbox and alert only for that. Keep the rest of your mail on a schedule.

faq.question: Does Lazur work on Windows?
faq.answer: No. Lazur runs on macOS, on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, but it is not available yet.

faq.question: Is there a free trial?
faq.answer: Lazur has a Pro trial with no credit card. The trial starts when you first open the app. Check the pricing page for current plan details.

costs.title: Lost first conversations
costs.text: A buyer who fills out a form often talks to more than one agent. The first useful reply tends to get the next question, the showing time, and the early trust. If your reply arrives after another agent's, you may be the second choice in the buyer's mind.

costs.title: Weekends you spend catching up
costs.text: The Bureau of Labor Statistics says schedules for brokers and sales agents often include evenings and weekends. If a lead arrives on Saturday and you reply on Monday, you spend the weekend cold. Restarting the conversation then takes more effort than one quick reply would have.

costs.title: Hours you already lose
costs.text: NAR's 2026 member profile reports a median week of 35 hours for all Realtors, and 30 hours for sales agents. Lead work competes with those hours. Slow replies push follow-up into your evenings, which is when you have the least time for it.

costs.title: No backup when you work solo
costs.text: BLS reports that 55% of brokers and 54% of sales agents are self-employed. Most of them have no teammate reading the inbox during a showing. A slow reply on a solo schedule becomes a missed lead, not a handoff.

costs.title: Spending on the wrong fix
costs.text: Without a reply log, you cannot see where the delay sits. You guess. Guesses lead to buying a tool when the real fix may be a notification setting. That costs money and still leaves the gap open.

causes.title: Notifications set on the wrong mailbox
causes.text: In Mail, notification alerts are chosen in Mail > Settings > General, in the New message notifications pop-up. If your lead mailbox is not the one selected there, new mail can arrive without a banner or a sound. You may check the app and still miss the lead for hours.

causes.title: A Focus that hides the lead account
causes.text: A Focus can limit notifications to Allow Some People or Allow Some Apps. It can also use a Mail filter that decides which accounts appear during that Focus. A showing Focus set up long ago can quietly hide the mailbox that gets your leads.

causes.title: Checking mail in batches
causes.text: Many agents check mail at set times. That habit fits newsletters. It does not fit buyer inquiries, which lose value while they wait. A batch check can turn a quick reply into a next-day reply without anyone noticing.

causes.title: Leads arriving in several places
causes.text: A portal, a website form, a text, and a voicemail transcript can each hold a buyer. Each place has its own habits. The one you check least becomes the one that gets the slowest replies. Lead sources multiply faster than most agents track them.

causes.title: Writing every reply from scratch
causes.text: Typing a new first reply each time costs minutes you do not have on a busy day. Agents often wait to reply until they have time to write something perfect. A saved template or a short holding reply removes that wait.

causes.title: No one covers when you are out
causes.text: BLS says many real estate jobs run on irregular hours, and most agents are self-employed. When you are on a showing, nobody else reads the inbox. Without a plan for that gap, the lead waits until you return.

fixes.title: Pick one lead mailbox
fixes.text: Choose a single mailbox for portal and website form mail if your setup allows it. Forward or route lead mail there rather than spreading it across accounts. One mailbox is easier to alert on, check, and measure.

fixes.title: Turn on alerts for that mailbox
fixes.text: In Mail, open Mail > Settings > General and look at the New message notifications pop-up. Choose the lead mailbox there. Send a test message from another account and confirm the banner appears.

fixes.title: Allow Mail through your showing Focus
fixes.text: Open the Focus you use for showings. Set notifications to Allow Some Apps and add Mail. Then check that the lead account is not filtered out in the Mail Focus setting. Test it once before a busy day.

fixes.title: Save three Gmail templates
fixes.text: Write a first reply that asks one question and offers a time. Write a showing time request and a check-in note. Save each as a Gmail template, then send yourself a test. A template turns a long wait into a quick reply.

fixes.title: Add a Shortcut that runs on email
fixes.text: Shortcuts on Mac can run when an email arrives, using an Email trigger. Start with a notification action. Keep Allow Running When Locked off for alerts you need to see, since Apple says that setting stops the notification.

fixes.title: Keep a reply log in Google Sheets
fixes.text: Log each lead's source, arrival time, and first reply time. Subtract arrival from reply, then format the result as a duration. After a few weeks, sort by the gap and fix the slowest source first.

fixes.title: Send holding replies on busy days
fixes.text: When you cannot give a full answer, send a short note. Say you are with a client and will follow up with specific times. Keep it under three sentences, and do not guess at price, availability, or terms.

fixes.title: Use Lazur for the wording and the settings
fixes.text: Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask what a buyer wants from the message on screen. Ask Lazur to draft a short first reply, then edit it. Hold fn to dictate a longer reply. Ask Lazur to walk you through the Mail settings, one click at a time.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Measure the gap
plan.text: Create a sheet with columns for lead name, source, arrival time, first reply time, and reply gap. Log every lead that comes in today, including the ones you answered quickly. Do not change any settings yet.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Fix the alerts
plan.text: Open Mail > Settings > General and choose your lead mailbox in the New message notifications pop-up. Send a test message from another account. Confirm the banner shows up before you move on.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Set your showing Focus
plan.text: Open the Focus you use for showings. Set notifications to Allow Some Apps and add Mail. Check the Mail filter so the lead account is not hidden during that Focus.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Write the templates
plan.text: Write a first reply, a showing time request, and a check-in note. Save each as a Gmail template. Send one test of each to yourself, and read the result before you trust it.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Test a Shortcut and compare
plan.text: Build a Shortcut with an Email trigger and a notification action. Send a test email to confirm it fires. Keep Allow Running When Locked off for alerts you need. Then compare your log with the Day 1 numbers.
